George McGovern in 1972 is a classic example of the difference between intense enthusiasm within a movement and broad appeal in a general election.

McGovern generated enormous excitement among young people, antiwar activists, students, and the newly enfranchised 18-to-20-year-olds after the voting age was lowered to 18. His campaign represented something genuinely new in Democratic politics: opposition to the Vietnam War, skepticism toward the establishment, civil rights, greater openness in the party, and a much larger role for grassroots activists.

The result was catastrophic. Nixon won about 61% of the popular vote to McGovern's 37.5% and carried 49 states. McGovern carried only Massachusetts and the District of Columbia.

There is an interesting lesson here that remains relevant today: primary enthusiasm can actually conceal general-election weakness. The people most motivated to attend rallies, volunteer, donate, and vote in primaries tend to be much more politically engaged—and sometimes more ideological—than the much larger population that appears in November.

The crux of BTS' protest is not "we are artists who happen to be Asian and we want to be treated equally", it's "as Asian artists who emulate Black artists and music, we want to be considered equal to the white artists who do the same".

This isn't projection, this was explicit to their origin as a group. These seven men were, as teenagers, originally assembled into a rap-focused group by a Korean entertainment company. They were assigned personas, outfits (including durags and chains), and hairstyles (including cornrows and perms) to mimic those of popular Black artists. American Hustle Life, one of their many reality programs available for free on YouTube, follows the BTS members to LA where they learn from Black artists (including Coolio) how to emulate Black American style. 

After building an audience in SE Asia, they would later move away from this "Black" concept as they expanded their target audience internationally, allowing members to drop their "tough guy" personas in favor of a more "soft boy" approach. This approach was extremely successful globally. 

Today, BTS' latest album (Arirang) was written and produced by a team of roughly 20 people, and sounds like it. It represents a return to BTS' origin concept, reflecting their rap, hip-hop, and R&B influences. It will be one of the top selling albums of the year. 

I agree with BTS, no artist - of any origin - has done a better job appropriating, industrializing, and profiting from Black music this year.

The question "what is pop?" is also a live one for fans of indie pop.  This music is done by artists on their own without a record label or with only a very tiny record label.  We contend with the purely musical question "when is it indie pop and when is it indie rock?"  Both styles will usually employ the same assortment of instruments.  Aside from a few reasonably reliable guidelines, i.e., if there's an extended instrumental break it's probably rock and if the artist's focus is mostly on the songcraft it's probably pop, the judgment is inevitably subjective.  Long ago the word "pop" was split up from the general qualification of "popular" rather than "arty" and not always for insidious racial reasons.

To be sure, the recording/music industry is guilty of historical racism, profiting through exclusion and appropriation. Real musicians, however, do not self-select, exclude, and appropriate in such a manner.  Music, and its genre distinctions, are fluid and constantly in flux. 

Musicians find inspiration. Musicians adopt. Musicians incorporate. Musicians pay homage to.

comments.body:
All the PE firms mentioned in the article are in or close to the category of mega-funds, meaning they are in the very top tier of assets under management (AUM). This makes the characterization of the entire industry as if all PE funds, of any size, in the same situation. That is correct as a general statement as the important metric of DPI (Distributions to Paid In Capital) are below historical levels. Institutional investors will not invest in new funds without enough coming back from old funds. Although borrowing rates are up, they are still low by long-term comparisons. 

The doubling of backlog is also relative to more active past periods, but there are now many more PE funds but many fewer publicly listed companies as the PE industry has become a more attractive owner for many businesses. Most of these companies will be sold, and if quick flips are not the order of the day, that does not mean the future value of the companies will not provide adequate returns. The numbers are also distorted by the fast rise and fall of software companies as AI rose to prominence.  

Overall, PE ownership is better governance and better shareholder value, the effective shareholders being mostly institutional investors like endowment funds and pensions funds. It may be the misperception of the general public and media that all PE funds are rapacious and a blight on society, but the companies they own still need to sell to customers. Public companies are not much different.

The problem with your hopes with Predictive Processing Theory is the same one that has dogged the rise of neuroscience - all of the important and useful aspects of your model are theory, rather than demonstrated fact. And neuroscience is especially complicit in blurring the line between theory and fact.Neuroscience researcher David Eagleman typifies this 'slight of hand' confabulation: One of his studies show that people whose names are similar to the word dentist (Donna, Dennis, etc.) disproportionately choose dentistry as a vocation. That's a fact. He goes on to say they do so because of the narcissism of having one's name associated with a prestigious occupation. That's pure, unsubstantiated theory. 
Neuroscience is rife with attributions of various patterns of brain activity as signifiers of important behavioral consequences - presented as fact, rather than theoretical suppositions. Strip current neuroscience of its theoretical suppositions, and what is left is mostly a much less utilitarian collection of 'stupid human tricks'

comments.body: While the author makes a thoughtful analysis of therapy's effectiveness, he relies on his perspective heavily, leaving out elements that are equally as important. I am a licensed clinical social worker, and we practice differently than psychoanalists. We see the inner worlds of individuals inextricably woven with their environments. Yes, childhood experiences pave pathways that are foundational to how we perceive the world. And so too does poverty, oppression, abuse, and our climate crisis. Society's institutions shape our beliefs in ourselves, others, and inform how we think, feel, and behave. A clinican can't isolate one factor as the cause of "disorder", a term the DSM5 uses to describe a client's experience. The very term reveals its bias. Whose disorder? Which leads to "what causes this disorder?" "What fixes it?" In social work, you can not separate out the individual from society. We live within systems that enhance and burden us. If I am physically abused and the police and legal system don't believe me, how helpful is it to challenge my fears if the systems meant to protect instead side with the abuser? Social work seeks to understand the experiences of the individual and address unjust institutions within society. Neurobiology has increased our understanding of our experience; but by focusing soley on this, we place the burden of wellbeing on the shoulders of those most vulnerable. To be helpful, we must also work toward the well-being of society and social justice.

Bulletin for Bruni: the future is always worth discussing... and Nolan’s ‘Odyssey,’ is, despite its deep immersion in the past, about the future.

Joseph Campbell, the author of 'The Hero with a Thousand Faces,' taught that the function of myth was to awaken and direct the vital energies. Ideology, on the other hand, has the opposite effect. It deadens and blocks them. Homer's 'Odyssey' is myth. Nolan's is ideology. 

Nolan's film is an ideological show trial right out of Bolshevik Russia. 

His theme is not how a man skilled in all ways of contending - a hero - learns to overcome his inner demons and is thus equipped to return home and restore justice and order. Rather, he is systematically diminished, derided, and undermined, and finally, as expiation, consigned with his wife to ritual death. and - this the key point - opens the way for a new elite to assume control. 

Does our civilization awaken, revitalize and properly direct the energies of its boys and men? On the evidence, No. A culture that abuses its men at every opportunity, at birth, in school, on the job, in family court, yet demands that each one be prepared to sacrifice his life for the same culture-- that is not a culture with a future.

Jackson threatened to send in Federal troops to enforce the "Tariff of Abomination" when Calhoun said that tariffs would not be collected in Charleston, harbour. 

It took wars to unite the country. Attention to real and imagined domestic "enemies" - exactly to what - altered continuously. It might be useful to think again of the United States to be a compact between states with certain powers, e.g., national defence, foreign affairs, including foreign trade, and enforcement of the Constitution, to be exclusively in the federal domain and most other functions of government reserved for the states. 

Strife today might be summarized as a much larger federal role due to the nature of world affairs requiring a large standing military and non-military functions devoted to international relations with attendant expenditures. The domestic role of the federal government might be confined to ensuring the unimpeded flow of trade and people between the states and enforcement of Constitutional guarantees pertaining to civil rights and liberties - and not to the wording of the Declaration of Independence. 

 If unhappy with the "sate of affairs", people can move from State to State.

My experience with UPS was similar in that no matter how many supervisors I spoke with, no matter how many times I was assured the delivery instructions said, take the elevator to second floor, my 32lb box was left in the lobby. It is expensive to live in all boroughs of NYC, Mr Mayor, you want to be trusted and respected by all New Yorkers, I sincerely hope that you can live up to your promises.

comments.name: Casual Cook

comments.name: AKJersey

comments.name: Valpo

comments.name: Keith Elrod

And don’t think for one moment Amazon won’t move its distribution centers out. Beso is not wealthy because he is stupid. He is wealthy because he is a good businessman. And if you can’t live in New York City on $20 an hour then don’t live in New York City. Does anyone there have just good old common sense?

comments.name: Ec
comments.body:
Good on the Mayor to pick this fight. Deliveries should not be the wild west - between rental trucks unloading to the not-Amazon delivery teams, to the not-Amazon "wagon bikes" clogging the sidewalks they act like they own, to the dangerous, heedless, no-name e-bike cargo carriers, the entire NYC delivery system needs to be regulated, insured, and enforced. 

How about using the good ol' US Postal Service?

comments.name: Molise
comments.body: I support the union.  Too many problems arise when private contractors get involved.  One of them being that they are not as careful about delivering your package.

comments.name: Kris Kringelov
comments.body:
I’d love to know the actual hit to Amazon’s margins if subjected to these regulations. If it is significant, analysts at the investment banks that cover the stock will be doing the work. If they are not, then they don’t believe this will impact Amazon’s earnings per share, and that will tell you whether abandonment of NYC distribution centers is a real threat. Without this information, I still have a strong hunch that online retailers will stick with the largest market in the country. 

Any biz reporter at NYT or WSJ will have access to this. 

And if these regulations require our fellow citizens to go around the corner for a bagel, so be it. I know there are plenty of items you can’t get in NYC anymore, but I see plenty of delivery guys enter my building with little brown bags from a local deli.  Can’t see this helps anyone outside of GLP-1 manufacturers.

Delcy Rodríguez is, as the Venezuelans would say, “El mismo musiú con diferente cachimba.”  It translates to “the same person with a different pipe” meaning “same old story, new packaging.”

Nothing has changed for the people of Venezuela.

comments.name: JERRY LEVY
comments.body: We can't do everything at once. I get it. Right now Iran has to be completed first, but Venezuela is a huge problem and it must be solved

comments.name: Diane
comments.body:
Europe, I understand, is heating up faster than any other continent. 

Reporting to date usually lacks any insight into why this is true. Additionally, reporting on massive heat waves fails to discuss the reasons for the heat. Climate change is here. Worse, in the U.S. the anticipated build out of massive AI data centers, some whose gas turbines producing electricity for the center will add pollution equivalent to 360,000 cars annually, is ignored.

Something’s got to give. Reporting should always include expert opinions on climate change effects, how they are generated and why these effects are making the world hotter. Reporting should also include interviewing government officials and corporate enterprises about what is happening and what can and should be done about it.

Lacking background and deep inquiry into cause and effects regarding the changing climate is shortchanging readers and entire populations as this crisis deepens and answers are sorely needed as to why, what and how to cope.

comments.name: Globulus Rift
comments.body:
I've noticed that the people I know who were climate change deniers and got angry and indignant about what they called a climate change conspiracy have gone deathly quiet on the subject now. 

It's winter here in Australia and a very mild one. I'm not looking forward to summer one bit - I think we're in for a shocker as well.

comments.name: State College Graduate
comments.body:
Why do so many writers use the term “bracing” when describing heat waves. 

Is it because the word “wave” is in the phrase? Like when an ocean wave comes at you? 

My fellow humans in Europe: Take it from a Californian, you don’t “brace” for a heat wave! You are not in the ocean. You go out and buy an air conditioner!  If it lies dormant for 11 months of the year, then great!  Make a nice cover for it and let it lie dormant, just like your winter holiday decorations may. 

But there is no bracing for a heat wave! You either leave your hot home and spend days at a cooling center, or travel to a cooler city if you can afford that, or you buy an air conditioner.

There are portable A/Cs and window A/Cs.  There are videos online of how to install them if you can’t find someone to do that work. The portable ones are the simplest to install and store away for next year.  

Would you “brace” for the winter? Of course not. You would prepare for the longs months of winter. Now you have to prepare for the heat too. It will be back next year!

comments.name: ManBearPig
comments.body: Planet Earth is very sick. Doctors (climatologists) know quite well what's wrong with the patient. The problem is that few want to hear the obvious cure because it's rather unpalatable in the short term.

comments.name: Tina
comments.body:
The Water Wars are beginning.

Already in parts of Europe, in the more remote, cooler locations, holiday homes are being sabotaged to deter holiday visitors from depleting the scarce water resources essential to the locals who live in those locations year round.

In years to come, the rich will colonise those regions able to sustain comfortable life, wherever they are on Earth; ironically, other regions will be peopled by those better evolved and adapted to survive in, hot water-scarce climates - those from Africa and Asia, mainly.

Those not well adapted and who are not in the top 20% of the wealth demographic (poor whites initially and then middle class whites) will lead increasingly painful and miserable lives, withering and eventually dying out.

This will happen over the next 50-100 years.

comments.name: Tizzy
comments.body: Please stop calling it a Heat Dome. It has been in the mid 90's ( 33-38 cel) since the beginning of June. Every single day. We live in the Luberon, Provence France. This is the new normal.

comments.name: Tina
comments.body:
The saddest part of all this is that Europe’s suffering will inwardly fill Trump with glee, such is his envy-driven bitterness and resentment toward the Old Countries.

If you share Trump’s insecurities, feel free to call it TDS.

comments.name: from

When you go to bed, slip it under your pillow as you sleep. That way, you cool your pillow and flip as necessary for instant relief.

comments.name: Marrocus
comments.body: Time to admit defeat, claim victory, and move on.

comments.name: Gene
comments.body: The best thing that's ever happened to the regime brutalizing and slaughtering the people of Iran, is Trump jumping into their trap.

comments.name: Blues
comments.body: Truly the Iranians sound more reasonable than Trump.

comments.name: Abe
comments.body:
The United States and Israel seem the far more radicalized party to this conflict.     Not a fan of Iran or any religion based regime as seen there and in Israel, but let’s not forget:    The United and Israel started this war, not Iran.     It seems reasonable they would want to be compensated for the damage done to their country via tolls on Hormuz.
Similar tolls are paid in other places.  
Iran has been under crippling sanctions for decades, and never once shut down Hormuz.  
Trump and Israel start bombing them in the middle of negotiations…..

comments.name: Robert Bell
comments.body:
For anyone who remains confused when Trump tells us "talks are ongoing and we will have a deal" let me simplify it for them.

The only talks now going on are between Iran and Oman on how to reach a "profit sharing" agreement between the two nations on how to split tolls on ships passing through the Staits of Hormuz, In perpetuity! 

When agreement is reached Iran will reach out to us and present that agreement as condition #1 in any negotiation and it will be non negotiable.  It is the way will receive REPARATIONS from us and our allies for the damage done to them.  

Of course, Trump will not initially agree to this and likely launch more air strikes but as we have seen to date the regine in charge in Iran now and for any reasonable foreseeable future is hard hard line.  They are , literally, willing to see the last civilian on Iranian soil killed by the United States and Israel and still will not "surreneder."

We have ourselves caught in a bear trap. And, Trump cannot bluster or bomb his way out of it. This is simply going to be like Viet Nam in the end. We expend our national treasure in a failed cause and leave a loser in the eyes of our enemy, our friends and any clear thinking citizen. The 28% of Americans who support his conduct of the war must be on acid.

comments.name: Joshua Kline
comments.body:
The ancient state of Iran has a sense of realpolitik which the upstart real estate developer Donald Trump clearly lacks.  He has painted himself into a corner, and Iran knows it.  Running short on weapons, popularity sinking, and midterms approaching, Iran is making harsh demands which, even taken in ones or twos, spell defeat for Trump's ill-considered gamble. 

 Anyway Trump turns it, it looks like no way out.  His ill-defined goals were brushed aside or painted over in the MOU, which anyway collapsed.  Now, his only recourse is more missiles and more bombs, but his allies are running as short on defensive missiles to curb Iran's inevitable response as Trump is on words to continue fooling the American people into believing that success is right around the corner.  The only hope is that this debacle will curtail other similar adventures, such as with Cuba, Greenland, and, for that matter, my own country of Canada.

comments.name: John Panzer
comments.body:
Trump’s foreign policy is a masterclass in performative projection masking total strategic incompetence.

By starting a conflict he couldn't sustain—largely as a desperate distraction from the Epstein files—he succeeded only in handing Iran absolute leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and world energy markets. Now, while global prices surge and everyday Americans pay the price, his response is to claim he is "low-keying it." In reality, the entire world knows the truth: he has run low on critical munitions and exhausted his military options.

Iran reads him like a book. Tehran knows he is far more terrified of inflation numbers hitting right before the midterm elections than he is capable of playing long-term geopolitics. Because he refuses to accept any strategic deal that makes him personally look weak or forces him to admit error, he is trapped in a corner of his own making.

This isn't strength; it is profound, dangerous weakness masquerading as toughness, and the rest of the world is watching him get outplayed at every turn.

comments.name: Kerry Landon-Lane
comments.body:
It’s illogical that Iran would make the touted deal with Oman. Why would Iran halve its stupendous Hormuz weapon. 

Iran would wish to maintain the weapon’s potency simply by not using it. It’s Iran’s nuclear bomb many times over. 

But the weapon can be also used by America as leverage in negotiations toward a safer region. A grand opportunity is not being recognized and seized. 

Unfortunately, we have an American president at a loss of what to do. And, none around him think straight.

comments.name: Olof
comments.body: After all is said and done, the conclusion will be that none of this was necessary and none of it will come to any good.  All these people who died, and the land, water, and environment, will suffer for no good reason.  It's a shame.  A real shame.

comments.name: K
comments.body: I wonder what “A brutal government behind us” truly means to them outside of this war.

comments.name: M H

Most military experts believe bombing campaigns rarely work; even regular citizens who hate a regime will turn their anger toward those who bombed their children’s schools, universities, power plants, pharmaceutical factories, and desalination plants. 

There has been no regime change, and a vital, highly strategic global waterway (which was free before the war) is now controlled by the regime. 

What a mess!

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: The Trump administration is gambling with civilian lives. Even to a casual observer it was obvious the Iranian regime could not be defeated by air power alone with unarmed civilian protesters supposedly left to take on the military might of the IRGC like lambs to the slaughter. Trump's promise to come to the aid of anti-regime protesters was nothing but false hope. Iranian civilians are paying the price for a delusional US administration that sees hardly a day without juvenile distractions and shenanigans that are devastatingly trashing the reputation of the US as a superpower.

comments.name: Craig Curie
comments.body: I agree, we're not hearing enough about the impact on the people in Iran. No one wants this war: only vindictive egotistical leaders. So let them fight it out between themselves (maybe in front of the White House). Leave the rest of us in peace.

comments.name: Ger

He should be applauded for turning around a dilapidated city with a limited future. You see many beautiful young Spanish people walking the streets and they look proud of their town - some are from other parts of Spain but they come to a city because of what it has to offer. Some of the food is overpriced for what you get - what city doesn't have that, but there are gems tuck away on the fringe of Malaga that I will go back to and recommend to others.  Viva Malaga.

comments.name: David

But tourists love it because it is set up for them - the city has set its course on this path of tourism fulfillment and it is obvious by the numbers that visit it. Remember also that this coast line is the expat center of Europe residentially, so it's not hard to understand the focus.

comments.name: cogito

comments.name: Pierre

The costs of eating or a drink in the centre went that high up that Malagueños mainly do not go to the centre at all. Besides that it is almost noit possible to hear Spanish in the centre. And yes, it was mentioned , the Inner country has a lot to offer but also I will not say where to prevent it will be destroyed also.

comments.name: Blue Green

Sounds as bad as the US House & Senate.

Where about more youthful leaders.

articles.title: Imports Don’t Depress Economic Growth
articles.summary: Pundits mistake an accounting operation for economic reality.

comments.name: Anthony Dolanski
comments.body: What is better, imports or exports? Imports are spending, exports are revenues. Life is better when generating sales.

comments.name: michael Reville
comments.body: Imports don't subtract from growth.   That's true.   Imports might add to growth because of US value added through the supply chain.  But ultimately, at the same price, more value is credited to GDP by domestically produced goods.   This is inescapable.  Like everything else, however, there is more to the story, the most significant being opportunity cost.  If cheap widgets are produced in the US, the labor dedicated to producing those widgets would not be deployed to produce higher value goods or services, especially in a tight labor market, where higher labor costs increase pressure to import goods that might otherwise be manufactured in the US.

comments.name: Brett D
comments.body:
GDP is kind of made up nonsense anyway. Since the 1950's we went from one person working to raise a household to it taking two people working. 

It caused a dramatic decline in standard of living that killed the birth rate but it was great for the GDP because now you have more people working.

GDP effectively values leisurely time at $0 so the way to maximize GDP is have everyone working 24/7.

comments.name: DAN WOJCIK
comments.body: Think the writer is mixing Gross Domestic Product with Gross Domestic Expenditures.

comments.name: Diane Thorton
comments.body:
Mr. Hebert - thank you for the well-written article and the concise, easily understood explanation of the topic. Always enjoy your contributions!

(PS - please tell David Sr. that Dawn and her Dad say hello!!)

comments.name: Richard Norman
comments.body: "Imports Don’t Depress Economic Growth"  ????  Sending the jobs over seas certainly does.

comments.name: Steven Daniel
comments.body:
Mr. Hebert, no less an economic light in the darkness, Mr. Trump, disagrees with you.

 If we have a "trade deficit" with a nation they are our "enemy" and punishing  tarrifs are required. 

Conversely, if we have a trade surplus, such as with Brazil, they are still an "enemy" and punishing tariffs are required. 

As you can see Mr. Trump has a deep understanding of these situations.

May I respectfully as that you fact check you pieces with Mr. Trump before you publish them?

comments.name: Michael Lowery
comments.body: Similarly, massive government spending is not subtracted from GDP to give a clean picture of the economy under the Laffer Curve. That's the real scandal. Pour $7 trillion in BidenDollars into the economy over 4 years, and GDP YOY looks terrific. That's your Shumer/Pelosi bragging rights, the nuclear torpedo in the side of the great US Ship of State, which the financial fish-wrappers have never understood. Then, ultra-low-IQ Repubs in Congress get blamed for high interest rates and the meteoric rise in prices. Democrats set the trap, and Republicans fall into it.

comments.name: Mochilero
comments.body:
The US contributed to these tragic problems by our precipitous withdrawal.

But by far more serious in terms of consequences was our decision to go in there in the first place.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: I just read all of the comments about this column. Almost all of them say that America does not have a moral responsibility toward Afghan women. I disagree but I also agree that the men of Afghanistan are the root of the problem. I feel sympathy but I don't feel guilt. Some problems are beyond our ability to solve.

comments.name: Liam
comments.body:
Former National Security Advisor H.R. McMaster called the February 2020 U.S.–Taliban Doha Agreement a "surrender agreement" and a "capitulation agreement". The Taliban had demanded that the Afghan government be excluded from the talks, and the Trump administration caved and agreed. What did that signal to the Afghan army, security forces, and people? That the US would not be defending them, which then went on to become a self-fulfilling prophecy as the state crumbled in mere days after the first city fell in 2021. 

Trump had 11 months between the February 2020 signing of the "surrender" and his exit from office in January 2021 - time which he completely wasted and did NOTHING to assure an orderly exit which would have protected as many Afghans as possible with refugee status. Instead, he and his sycophants remain perfectly gleeful to blame the disasterous exit entirely on Biden. All Trump ever cares about is the blame game.

comments.name: Craig Mason
comments.body:
We had a moral responsibility to build a state, which required that all of our resources be dispensed openly by proper procedures -- to create a legal-rational state.

Instead, we strengthen feudal and personalist ties, which assured there would be no state when we left.

In my view, we should have given only women the vote for the first two election cycles and then enfranchised men as they qualified as respecting women's rights.

We wasted 20 years.

comments.name: Wayfaring Stranger
comments.body:
Believe me when I say I feel your pain. The desertion of America from Afghanistan is the blackest of marks on America’s soul. Mislabeling our involvement as another failed forever war, was a political crime, something we are used to since January 2025, crimes against humanity are part and parcel of this administration. Trump negotiated our desertion with our enemy and excluded the legitimate Afghan government in all negotiations and signed an agreement with little regard for the consequences of returning the country back to the taliban. The dye was cast when he released thousands of taliban prisoners and removed thousands of American troops
undermining all that our occupation had accomplished. Life is truly luck and happenstance and you have earned and are entitled to your happiness and success. I too am sad for the lives of women held in bondage by a draconian government of men. If we had held on, the dreams and lives of so many women could have been fulfilled and our involvement would have been rewarded because we were witnessing in real time the fruits of our presence. May they forgive us, though we may not be able to forgive ourselves.

comments.name: Silas Campbell
comments.body: We are constantly told women can do anything men can do.  If the women of Afghanistan didn't want to live under the Taliban they should have gotten a weapon and fought for the alternative government.

comments.name: Ben Farrell
comments.body: Afghanis, male and female, have that moral responsibility to themselves to make their own lives better. If that means turning away from oppressive theocracy, then it is their duty to do so. It is not America's job.

comments.name: Sam M
comments.body: The U.S. owes the women of Afghanistan nothing. These people had the opportunity to throw off the yoke of Sharia law off and instead chose to capitulate to the Taliban. The U.S. trained and armed and paid the Afghan military for years. If you are unwilling to fight for your own freedom and rights, you do not deserve them. If the women of Afghanistan want to blame someone, start with their fathers, brothers, husbands and  sons.

articles.title: What America Owes to Afghan Women
articles.summary: Five years after giving up on Afghanistan, America still has a responsibility to the country’s women.

comments.name: ML
comments.body:
Perhaps we aren't actually afraid of autonomous vehicles. Perhaps we don't actually fear raw masses of circuitry and code. Perhaps what we are actually afraid of is feeling at the mercy of yet another company pushing a "disruptive" technology with inadequate testing, a focus on revenue over lives, and a propensity for distorting data to its benefit.

I don't really see this angle in this article, and I think it's a sorely missing one. Most people I've spoken to aren't alarmed by autonomous vehicles in the abstract. They're alarmed by profit-driven companies aggressively seeking to push technologies on us, without regard to individual danger or societal well-being.

comments.name: Alan.
comments.body: Being a driver who drives defensively not offensively I'm constantly trying to figure out what other drivers are going to do as far as affecting my safety.  When the time comes that autonomous cars are perfect (wishful thinking) I belief will be the end of traffic accidents and jams,  simply because all vehicles on the road would be communicating with one another.  Vehicles will tell each other what they plan to do and the other vehicles will let them do it safely making for a seamless flow of traffic instead of what we now experience.  I know it won't happen in my lifetime but it is a nice thought to be able to get in one's auto and NOT DRIVE  but setback and enjoy the scenery.

x86 is public and technically anyone could build a simple chip. Intel & AMD have cross-licensing agreements on Intel's extensions like MMX & SSE along with AMD64. The extensions aren't public and it's probably impossible to build a chip without violating someone's patent.

For at least 30 years, the actual instruction set hasn't really mattered. All CPUs have a translation layer that converts their CISC (like x86) into an internal RISC architecture. As more cache and execution units get stuffed in, the translation takes up a smaller and smaller % of the transistor budget.

Most code is written in high-level languages and can be recompiled for any chip architecture. I don't trust Washington to get regulation right for an issue nobody there understands. I don't know of any engineers in Congress besides Thomas Massie and he lost his primary.

Spain: the Volunteer Astronomy Observers of Spain maintains Eclipse Seguro (Eclipse Safety), an official regional vetting initiative specifically created to list verified, safe suppliers of eclipse glasses across Europe.
Major European bodies like the Royal Astronomical Society 
(RAS-UK) or national observatories issue safety guides that redirect viewers to verified manufacturers or optics distributors.

The American Astronomical Society has “The AAS Suppliers of Safe Solar Viewers & Filters” page that includes major European and United Kingdom manufacturers. The AAS collaborates internationally and verifies that European manufacturers meet standard lab certifications.
You can bypass third-party online sellers, and buy directly from long-standing European companies and AAS-listed manufacturers in Europe.
>Bresser (Germany)

comments.name: Sopan Deb
comments.body: This was a really fascinating piece to report on. A combination of performance art and nostalgia. There was a vulnerability to it that isn't there now, because we are more likely to curate it since we're so used to it. That probably speaks to why the Instagram account has become so popular.
